title: Ars Live: Ross Scott discusses the Stop Killing Games movement
gist: A short event promo for an August 11 Ars Live interview with Ross Scott, founder of the Stop Killing Games campaign, which began in 2024 after Ubisoft shut down The Crew's servers. The signal worth filing: the movement has collected millions of petition signatures and has already produced a European Commission parliamentary debate and response plus proposed legislation moving through the California legislature — a live regulatory threat to the games-as-a-service model, with Sony's decision to stop selling PlayStation discs cited as an aggravating factor.

themes.theme: Regulatory momentum on perpetual game access

insights.claim: The Stop Killing Games campaign has gathered millions of signatures on government petitions demanding legislation that guarantees some form of perpetual access to purchased games, either through continued centralized server support or an option for players to run their own servers.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A mandated end-of-life server or self-hosting obligation would add a permanent tail cost to every online-only title publishers ship.
insights.locator: Scott founded the Stop Killing Games movement in 2024

insights.claim: The campaign has already produced an official parliamentary debate and a formal response from the European Commission, plus proposed legislation working its way through the California legislature — moving it from consumer complaint to active policy in two of the industry's largest markets.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: EU plus California is effectively a global standard by default; watch the California bill text for the compliance cost that publishers would have to book.
insights.quote: The movement has already led to an official parliamentary debate and response from the European Commission and proposed legislation that is working its way through the California legislature.
insights.locator: Scott founded the Stop Killing Games movement in 2024

insights.claim: Ars Technica frames it as an open question whether the game preservation problem can actually be legislated away, signaling that the enforcement mechanics — not the political will — are the uncertain part.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Legislative momentum without a workable enforcement design usually yields disclosure requirements rather than hard obligations — the cheaper outcome for publishers.
insights.quote: whether or not this problem can really be legislated away
insights.locator: I'll be talking to Scott about how the movement came together

insights.claim: Ross Scott founded the Stop Killing Games movement in 2024 specifically in reaction to Ubisoft's decision to shut down the servers for The Crew, showing that a single publisher's sunset decision can catalyze cross-border regulatory action.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Server-sunset decisions now carry regulatory blowback risk, not just customer-service risk — a new consideration in live-service portfolio pruning.
insights.locator: Scott founded the Stop Killing Games movement in 2024

insights.claim: Sony's decision to stop selling PlayStation discs is feeding directly into the long-term game access debate, tying the hardware industry's shift to all-digital distribution to the preservation fight.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Removing the physical fallback strengthens the regulatory case; Sony's digital transition may accelerate the very rules that constrain it.
insights.quote: how recent moves like Sony’s decision to stop selling PlayStation discs are impacting the debate over long-term game access
insights.locator: We'll also discuss how recent moves

insights.claim: The two structural failure modes driving consumer anger are centralized online servers being shut down and critically acclaimed titles being digitally delisted so they can no longer be purchased or downloaded.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Any legislation will likely target these two mechanisms specifically — delisting policy and server EOL are the compliance surfaces to watch.
insights.locator: By now, any serious gamer is familiar
